The library uses the godotenv package for loading environment variables from a `.env` file. You can also set these environment variables manually in your deployment environment.
- `pgeventstore`: PostgreSQL implementation of `EventStore` with `Init` bootstrap and `StorageS` factory.
- AsyncSequential: handler runs outside any DB transaction; only short transactions are used to fetch events and to persist acks.
- FIFO: handler runs inside a transaction that remains open for the duration of the handler call; offsets are persisted at the end of the batch.
- Both are sequential and preserve event order per consumer-group.
- AsyncSequential auto-acks unhandled types and uses a dedicated, batched ack loop with contiguous-ack logic and gap bootstrap (handles streams starting at 0 or after retention).
- FIFO fetches only types with registered handlers and updates offsets once per batch inside the processing transaction.
- AsyncSequential provides bounded queues, non-blocking enqueue with backoff, adaptive sleeps, and deterministic channel-based shutdown.
- FIFO performs straightforward loop processing inside a transaction and sleeps between polls; it does not buffer work.
- Choose AsyncSequential when handlers can be slow or you want minimal lock time in the DB.

Four-dimensional scoping user_id / agent_id / run_id / app_id — enforced by physical isolation : one SQLite file per scope, rather than shared rows with a filter applied.

Single-pass ADD-only extraction One model call per write; memories accumulate and are never overwritten. Because nothing is rewritten, a bad extraction only introduces noise — it can never destroy a real fact.
Graph memory, always on Entity linking and multi-hop traversal live in the same SQLite file. No external graph database required.

Multimodal ingestion Accepts the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini image content shapes (plus audio). With a vision model configured it stores a description; without one it stores the reference — nothing is dropped.
Multi-signal retrieval Semantic + BM25 keyword + entity graph + temporal + tag, fused with calibrated relevance floors and a lexical fallback.
Temporal reasoning Observation dates, relative-time resolution, expiry semantics, and per-entity version chains.
Tiered memory Hot / warm / cold tiers with forgetfulness economics: low-value memories are demoted and compressed, never silently deleted.

Lossless compression (AIC) Compresses a memory into pointer + structured facts + content atoms . Numbers, dates, amounts and model numbers survive at every tier; expand() recovers the original text byte-for-byte and verifies its hash.
Hash-chained audit ledger A SHA-256 chain; verify_integrity() detects tampering and names the exact entry that changed.

|`memory_inject`|Context injection pipeline: query construction → four-path recall → RRF fusion → rerank → in-budget injection. Returns ready-to-inject text plus four quota ledgers. Prefer this over `recall` when you are preparing a prompt.|

|`recall_catalog`|Progressive disclosure, catalog level: returns title + one line + expansion cost only, never the body. Decide which are relevant, then expand 1–2 with `expand_memory` — injection cost drops from O(everything) to O(catalog + a few).|

|`expand_memory`|Progressive disclosure, expansion: one memory's body + unified envelope + graph neighbours + evidence chain. Pairs with `recall_catalog`; neighbours come from the knowledge graph, so "which modules did this decision affect" is answerable.|

|`memory_envelope`|Unified memory envelope: eight-class typing + four-dimensional scope + evidence chain + dual time axis + TTL + SPO structure. Omit `memory_id` for a whole-library eight-class distribution.|
|`memory_consolidate`|Three consolidation paths: episodic→semantic, episodic→procedural, failure→negative memory. Idempotent — the same source batch never generates twice.|

|`memory_metrics`|Metrics: Chat (5) + Working (4) + Coding (4). Honest by design — insufficient data returns `{value:null, status:"insufficient_data"}` rather than 0, because 0 and "no data" are different things.|

|`memory_cascade_delete`|Cascade delete: soft-delete the source → invalidate derived conclusions → clear the retrieval cache → mark dependent summaries stale. `hard=true` for physical delete; run `dry_run=true` first to see dependents.|

|`memory_mask`|Mask: replace the body with a placeholder but keep the record skeleton, preserving context length and prefix so KV-Cache reuse is not broken. Prefer this over delete when the user says "don't keep this". `action=unmask` reverses it.|

|`topic_summarize`|L3 topic summary: merge several L2 session summaries in one project into "where this project stands now". Merging is deterministic (goal newest, decisions accumulate, pending newest only). `persist=true` stores it and records `pointer.children`.|
|`memory_trace`|Pointer-chain backtracking: walk L3→L2→L1, returning each layer's content, the turn ranges it covers and its `message_ids`. Answers "which sentence did this conclusion come from".|

|`memory_hot_path`|Hot-path buffer: `action=enable` turns on async writes (the hot path only enqueues); `action=status` inspects the queue; `action=flush` waits for the queue to land — the read-consistency barrier you must pass before reading right after writing.|

This project is a starter kit that allows you to set up a RESTful API service that stores game leaderboards (scores) and exposes them via HTTP(s) methods/operations. A game developer can use this API service in their game and post new scores, get the top scores, find out the latest ones and more. A Unity client is also provided. You can read some of the thought process that drove the creation of this project in the blog post here.
One-click deployment via Azure ARM template is supported, click the button below to deploy the project in your Azure subscription using Azure Functions Consumption Plan.

The technology/architecture stack includes an Express Node.js app hosted on an Azure Function that talks to a Cosmos DB database via its MongoDB API). Azure Application Insights service is used to provide information and metrics regarding application performance and behavior. A Unity game engine client is also provided, with a relevant SDK to access the leaderboards API.

On the software side of things, Mongoose is used to facilitate interactions between the JavaScript code and the database whereas the frontend API calls are served by Express web framework. Also, the azure-functions-express package is used to facilitate the usage of Express framework within an Azure Function.

All requests to the leaderboards API **must** contain two headers on each request: `x-ms-client-principal-id` and `x-ms-client-principal-name`. If these values are missing, then the request will fail. The `x-ms-client-principal-id` should be unique for each user. Meaning, each time you use the same `x-ms-client-principal-id` for inserting a new score, this score will belong to the same user. The implemented leaderboards API does not impose any method to validate/verify these values, so you are free to implement whatever you like. However, App Service supports various authentication methods which automatically set the required headers, you can check them here. The Unity client sample in this repo contains code to set these headers with current user's details. For more details on authentication/authorization, please check the tech details file here.

Here you can see a short list/summary of all the operations that are supported, check here for full details and response samples. Some operations support skipping via a `skip` query string parameter, check the operations page for details.
|POST|https://**functionURL**/api/scores|Creates a new score. Post body has the format { "value":Integer value of the score, ... }. Returns the updated user details.|
|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/users/:userId|Gets a specific user's details, including top score and latest scores|
|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/user/scores/:count|Gets the top 'count' scores for logged in user sorted by score value|
|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/scores/top/:count|Gets top scores achieved in the game by all users, in descending order. This can include more than one score per user|
|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/users/maxscore/:count|Gets the scores achieved by each unique user, in descending order. Practically this includes the max score per single user|

|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/users/toptotaltimesplayed/:count|Gets the top 'count' users for all time in regards to the times they have played (i.e. number of times they have posted a new score).|
|GET|https://**functionURL**/api/users/surroundingbyscore/:userId/:count|Gets the surrounding users of the requested one, ordered by their max score|

|A path to the database file|`Sqlite3Database.FromPath(path)` finds `-wal` and `-journal` next to it, as SQLite does|
|The database file only, with no `-wal` or hot `-journal`|`Sqlite3Database.FromStreamWithNoJournal(database)`|
|The database file and its `-wal` file (WAL mode)|`Sqlite3Database.FromStreamWithWal(database, wal)`|
|The database file and its `-journal` file (rollback modes)|`Sqlite3Database.FromStreamWithJournal(database, journal)`|

`db.Header` has every field of the file's 100-byte database header, as read at open, such as the page size, the freelist, the schema cookie and the SQLite version that last wrote the file. `UserVersion` and `ApplicationId` are the values applications set with `PRAGMA user_version` and `PRAGMA application_id` to tell their databases apart:

* **`SqliteCorruptException`**: the file is malformed. `Check` names the consistency check that failed (the IDs are listed in docs/sqlite-checks), and `Page` and `Structure` say where, when known. Damage is reported where SQLite reports it: a malformed header or schema fails the open (in Lenient, a schema row that fails to load fails only the open of its table), a damaged b-tree fails the table's open or its row enumeration, and a bad value fails only the read of that value.

* **Rollback (DELETE, TRUNCATE, PERSIST).** A hot `-journal`, left by a write that never finished, is played back, so the database reads as it was before that write. This is what a writable SQLite connection does on open. A read-only SQLite connection instead refuses to read the database (`SQLITE_READONLY_ROLLBACK`). A journal that names a super-journal (a transaction across attached databases) is always played back; see Differences from SQLite.
* `GetTableDefinition()` also works on a `Sqlite3SchemaRow` from `GetTables()`, so a table's columns can be read without opening the table. It throws as described under Errors.
* **No locking.** The library takes no locks and assumes exclusive access (see Journal modes). Reading files while another process writes to them can return inconsistent data.
* **Hot journals are played back, not refused.** See Journal modes.
